content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Patch-Mix Transformers as an approach for unsupervised domain adaptation for Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures. The approach builds intermediate domains by weighted mixing of patches corresponding to images from the source and target domains and using attention maps to determine the contribution of each patch to the overall label space. The approach shows competitive results across a variety of unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper presents a new unsupervised domain adaptation approach for Vision Transformers which strongly outperforms prior work on the popular DomainNet dataset and provides competitive results on the other popular domain adaptation datasets (Office-31, OfficeHome, VisDA-2017). The PatchMix approach which combines attention weighting with a mixup strategy is intuitive and better reflects the contributions various parts of image should have on the downstream label. The authors do a thorough job with experimentation and test the various components of their approach. 

However, the narrative of the text does not seem to be well aligned with the experimental results presented. 
The effect of PatchMix vs the simpler Mixup alternative appears to be very moderate in the results presented (0.2) w/o error bars. 
The game-theoretic formulation of the intermediate domain is presented as a core contribution of this work, however its hard to determine the importance or relevance of this formulation. 
The presentation of the semi-supervised mixup loss in this work is hard to follow and empirically seems to be the most important proposal. 
This loss is not compared with losses presented in other mixup works and it is hard to distinguish which parts of the proposed loss represent new contributions to the literature.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The core ideas and contributions of this work are not clearly presented and easy to follow. The PatchMix approach definitely has novelty, and while the number of comparisons over the same model architectures is limited, the results over a variety of popular benchmarks lends credence to the quality of the evaluations. 

How this approach interacts with, builds upon and can be combined with prior work or future approaches is not readily apparent and is the drawback on the paper as is.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work contributes a novel approach to unsupervised domain adaptation field and has compelling results over challenging datasets. It also is designed for transformer architectures which have shown differences in robustness characteristics from convolutional architectures highlighted by most prior work. While the presentation of the approach and results can be greatly improved, the ability of approach to succeed in a variety of settings makes it of interest to the field.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an extension to ViT for the unsupervised domain adaptation problem on image classification. The main extension is a module, coined PatchMix, that mixes the patches from the source and target domains in what the authors call an intermediate domain. These mixed patches (intermediate domain), together with the original patches (from source and target domains) are the inputs to ViT. PatchMix basically performs a linear interpolation between the source and target patches and the linear parameter is a random variable that follows a Beta distribution. Moreover, the parameter of the Beta distribution is learnt such that the interpolation results in mixed patches (which can be thought as samples from an intermediate domain) that maximise the Cross Entropy between the source and target domains. In addition to the PatchMix module, the paper proposes (semi-supervised) loss functions that aim to minimise the Cross Entropy between the intermediate and both the source and target domains, both in the features and their (semisupervised for the target domain) labels. Since one term of the total loss maximises the CE, while the others minimise it, the authors motivate the problem as a minimax problem. Experiments in various benchmarks show the proposed approach outperforms previous works, especially on DomainNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
- The minimax formulation is novel and sensible.
- Numerical results across all experiments validate the benefits of the approach.

**Weaknesses**
- Game theoretical connections like using Nash equilibria as solution concept is loose (see comments below)
- The paper is not very clear (see comments below)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**
- The organisation could be improved. The authors repeat the same message multiple times, but they often miss the opportunity of starting with the intuition and making the concepts clearer. For example, it is repeated that PatchMix learns to sample and that tries to maximise the CE. However, it is not until the pseudocode in Appendix D, where it becomes crisp that the parameters of the Beta distribution are given by $\omega_3$.
- At the end of page 5, the authors refer to yellow and pink items, but it is not clear which are the pink items in Fig 3b.
- At the end of Sec. 3, it is not clear what the authors mean by "one-step otimization". Do they mean that they optimise the whole $\omega$ at every step (as opposed to optimising $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and $\omega_3$ by optimising one loss function each? If so, they have to prove the claim that such process leads to a Nash equilibrium (see comment on quality below).



**Quality**
- The numerical results are convincing.
- The derivation of the algorithm is loose. Although the motivation of the algorithm from a game theory point of view is OK, as there are multiple loss functions, Eq. (3) is expressed as $J(\omega)$, resulting in a scalarisation of the problem, whose solution is a Pareto point, but not necessarily a Nash equilibrium for general games. This seems to be a discrepancy with the text where they say they choose and find a Nash equilibrium as solution concept. How has this function been motivated? Can the authors prove the minimum of $J(\omega)$ is a Nash equilibrium? If that is not possible, it seems to me the authors should replace Nash equilibrium with Pareto point as solution concept.


**Minor comments**
- Some concepts of game theory doesn't seem to be accurate. For example, the authors refer to "the optimal Nash Equilibria", but it is not clear what they mean by "optimal" in this case.
- Title of Sec 3.1 is confusing since the section motivates the algorithm rather than performing its analysis.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a valid algorithm that improves the state-of-the-art for unsupervised domain adaptation on image classification. However, the paper lacks clarity and accuracy when establishing a connection with game theory.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors tackle the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation for image classification where the source images are labeled and target images are unlabeled. They propose to mix-up patches from source and target images to get an intermediate domain image. Then the learned patch mixing module tries to maximize the loss between the intermediate domain and source/target domains, while the feature extractor and the classifier try to minimize the loss between the intermediate domain and source/target domain. They validate the proposed method on public benchmarks: Office-31, OfficeHome, VisDA, and DomainNet. The claimed contributions are as follows:

C1. They propose a UDA framework by introducing an intermediate domain by patch-wise mixup.

C2. They propose PatchMix that mix-up patches from source and target domains.

C3. They propose two semi-supervised mixup losses for UDA.

C4. The proposed method shows favorable performance on public benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The problem they tackle, unsupervised domain adaptation is important.


However, this paper has critical weaknesses.

W1. The improvement compared to naïve mix-up is quite marginal. In Table 7, naïve mix-up shows 88.3% accuracy and the proposed method shows 88.5% accuracy (only 0.2 points gain). Given that the proposed method is very complicated compared to naïve mix-up, I do not see any reason to use the proposed method. Just adding a simple adversarial loss between source and target on top of mix-up might show similar or even higher accuracy than the proposed method.

W2. The improvement from the learned patch-mix is marginal. In Table 6, learning patch-mix shows 88.5% accuracy, and using the fixed hyperparameter shows 88.2% accuracy (0.3 points gain). 

W3. Technical contribution is weak. They formulate the UDA problem as a min-max game between patch-mixer and feature extractor/classifier without providing any reasonable motivation. Also, they propose to use a random mix-up ratio instead of using gradient reversal for UDA without any justification. Why don’t we use a simpler gradient reversal or GAN loss to solve the min-max game?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Because the proposed method gives marginal improvement compared to a naïve baseline, I would evaluate the quality low. The equations and text descriptions are too complicated without good motivations. Therefore, the clarity is also low. They just tweak the existing mixup and adversarial UDA a little bit and it results in marginal improvement. Therefore, I would evaluate the novelty low as well.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper does not show significant improvement compared to a naïve baseline and does not bring any good insight of the UDA problem. Therefore, I would like to recommend a rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new framework based on ViT, and PMTrans, to solve the unsupervised domain adaptation problem. This framework includes a new module, PatchMix, to build up an intermediate domain, and two semi-supervised mixup losses in the feature and label spaces.
The experimental results suppress the prior methods by a large margin.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ The experimental results suppress the prior methods by a large margin.
+ A new attempt to explore the UDA problem based on ViT.

Weaknesses
+ It is unfair to compare the ViT-based method with the methods with ResNet-based directly. It is difficult to verify whether the improvement is due to the method or the feature extraction network.
+ In Tab. 5, the role of $L_f$ is not obvious, and the main contributor to the result is $L_l$, i.e., the semi-supervised mixup loss in label space. However, this paper is not the first one to use it in semi-supervised-learning-or-DA tasks, e.g., [1] and [2].
+ In Tab. 7, the comparison between PatchMix and classical Mixup (+0.2%) cannot demonstrate that “PatchMix can capture the global and local mixture information better than the global mixture Mixup”, but demonstrates that the traditional Mixup is simple but effective.
+ Some typo errors, such as the quotation marks in Section 4.2.

[1] Berthelot D, Carlini N, Goodfellow I, et al. Mixmatch: A holistic approach to semi-supervised learning[J]. Advances in neural information processing systems, 2019, 32.
[2] Liang J, Hu D, Wang Y, et al. Source data-absent unsupervised domain adaptation through hypothesis transfer and labeling transfer[J]. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 2021.

content.title: PATCH-MIX TRANSFORMER FOR UNSUPERVISED DOMAIN ADAPTATION: A GAME PERSPECTIVE
content.abstract: Endeavors have been recently made to leverage the vision transformer (ViT) for the challenging unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) task. They typically adopt the cross-attention in ViT for direct domain alignment. However, as the performance of cross-attention highly relies on the quality of pseudo labels for the targeted samples, it becomes less effective when the domain gap becomes larger. We solve this problem from a game theory’s perspective with the model called PMTrans, which bridges the source and the target domains with an intermediate domain. Specifically, we propose a novel ViT-based module called PatchMix that effectively builds up the intermediate domain, i.e., probability distribution, by learning to sample patches from both domains based on the game-theoretical models. In this way, it learns to mix the patches from source and target domains to maximize the cross entropy (CE), while exploiting two semi-supervised mixup losses in the feature and label spaces to minimize CE. As such, we interpret the process of UDA as a min-max CE game with three players, including the feature extractor, classifier, and PatchMix, to find the optimal Nash Equilibria solution. Moreover, we leverage attention maps from ViT to re-weight the label of each patch by its importance, making it possible to obtain more domain-discriminative feature representations. We conduct extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, and the results show that PMTrans significantly surpasses the ViT-based and CNN-based SoTA methods by +1.4% on Office-31, +3.5% on Office-Home, and +17.7% on DomainNet, respectively.
